questions.stem: Which set includes the main domains assessed during routine developmental assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: Reflexes, skin color, temperature, and pulse

options.label: B
options.text: Immunization, feeding, sleep, and urine output

options.label: C
options.text: Gross motor, fine motor/vision, hearing/speech/language, and social development

options.label: D
options.text: Weight, height, head circumference, and blood pressure

options.label: E
options.text: Cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, and hepatic function

questions.correctAnswerText: Gross motor, fine motor/vision, hearing/speech/language, and social development
questions.initialExplanation: Developmental assessment is multidimensional and evaluates movement, hand/visual skills, communication, and social interaction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. General examination signs — Incorrect. Reflexes and vital signs may be important, but they do not replace domain-based developmental assessment.

- B. Health routines — Incorrect. These are relevant to history and care but do not cover the main developmental domains.
- C. Four developmental domains — Correct. These are the domains organized sheets.
- D. Anthropometry and blood pressure — Incorrect. These assess growth and physical health, not developmental skills.
- E. Organ systems — Incorrect. These are systems assessed in a general medical examination, not the core developmental domains.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gross motor: posture, head control, sitting, standing, walking, jumping.
- Fine motor/vision: reaching, grasping, pincer grip, visual fixation and tracking.
- Hearing/language: sound response, babbling, words, phrases, comprehension.
- Social: smiling, interaction, gestures, self-help, and play.

questions.stem: Which skill is classified mainly as a gross motor milestone?

options.label: B
options.text: Pointing to a picture in a book

questions.correctAnswerText: Walking independently
questions.initialExplanation: Gross motor development concerns control of large muscle groups and posture, including sitting, standing, walking, running, and jumping.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Transferring a cube — Incorrect. This is a fine motor/manipulative skill.
- B. Pointing to a picture — Incorrect. This involves communication and fine motor/visual coordination rather than gross motor control.

- C. Pincer grasp — Incorrect. This is a fine motor skill involving thumb and index finger.
- D. Two-word phrase — Incorrect. This is a language milestone.
- E. Walking independently — Correct. This requires postural control, balance, and coordinated large-muscle activity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gross motor milestones progress from head control to sitting, standing, walking, and higher-level locomotion.
- Assess symmetry, tone, posture, and quality of movement as well as the milestone itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following is primarily a fine motor milestone?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mature pincer grasp
questions.initialExplanation: Fine motor skills involve precise hand and finger movements, object manipulation, and visual-motor coordination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Walking upstairs — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.
- B. Unsupported sitting — Incorrect. This is a gross motor milestone requiring trunk control.
- C. Running — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.
- D. Hopping — Incorrect. This is a higher-level gross motor skill.

- E. Pincer grasp — Correct. The infant uses the thumb and index finger to pick up a small object.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fine motor milestones include reaching, grasping, transferring, pincer grip, scribbling, and drawing.
- Assess vision and hand use together; asymmetry or persistent failure to use one hand warrants evaluation.

questions.stem: Which finding belongs primarily to the hearing and speech-language domain?
questions.correctAnswerText: Babbling with consonant sounds
questions.initialExplanation: Hearing and language assessment includes responses to sounds, vocalization, babbling, understanding, gestures, words, and later phrases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Unsupported sitting — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.
- B. Pulling to stand — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.
- C. Consonant babbling — Correct. Canonical babbling is an important early communication milestone.
- D. Kicking a ball — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.

- E. Pincer grasp — Incorrect. This is fine motor development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hearing is foundational for speech-language acquisition.
- Assess both expressive language and receptive understanding.
- Delayed language should prompt hearing assessment as part of the evaluation.

source.raw: Developmental Assessment - red flags, PDF p.2

questions.stem: Which is an example of a social-development milestone?

options.label: C
options.text: Social smile in response to a caregiver

questions.correctAnswerText: Social smile in response to a caregiver
questions.initialExplanation: Social development includes reciprocal interaction, social smiling, recognition of familiar people, gestures, play, and relationships with peers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hand transfer — Incorrect. This is fine motor development.
- B. Rolling — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.
- C. Social smile — Correct. This reflects early social responsiveness.
- D. Stairs — Incorrect. This is gross motor development.

- E. Drawing — Incorrect. This is fine motor/visual-motor development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Observe eye contact, shared attention, gestures, imitation, and reciprocal interaction.
- Social development is assessed through interaction and play, not language alone.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the meaning of a developmental milestone listed at a particular age?

options.label: A
options.text: A child who reaches one milestone cannot have delay in another domain

options.label: B
options.text: Milestones are useful after school entry

options.label: C
options.text: Missing one milestone automatically confirms a specific neurological diagnosis

options.label: D
options.text: each healthy child must acquire the skill on the exact day of that age

options.label: E
options.text: It is a skill that most children are expected to demonstrate by that age, but it is not an inflexible deadline or diagnostic test

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a skill that most children are expected to demonstrate by that age, but it is not an inflexible deadline or diagnostic test
questions.initialExplanation: Milestones help structure developmental surveillance and identify possible concerns. They do not by themselves establish a diagnosis or replace standardized screening.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. No domain-specific delay — Incorrect. A child may have age-appropriate skills in one domain and delay in another.

- B. Only after school entry — Incorrect. Developmental surveillance begins in infancy.
- C. Automatic diagnosis — Incorrect. A missed milestone requires assessment, not an automatic diagnosis.
- D. Exact-day deadline — Incorrect. Development varies, and milestone ages are not exact dates.
- E. Most children, not a rigid deadline — Correct. CDC checklists focus on skills achieved by most children by the stated age and support discussion and early action.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Use milestones to guide surveillance and discussion.
- Use validated screening tools when indicated.
- Any developmental regression is particularly concerning and needs prompt evaluation.

## Early Infancy: 6 Weeks to 6 Months

questions.stem: At approximately what age does a social smile usually emerge?
questions.correctAnswerText: Around 6–8 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: A social smile in response to a familiar face or interaction generally appears by around 2 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 12 months — Incorrect. By this age, social communication includes gestures and interactive games.
- B. 2 years — Incorrect. This is far later than expected for social smiling.

- C. 9 months — Incorrect. This is later infancy, when reciprocal interaction and stranger anxiety may be evident.
- D. 6–8 weeks — Correct. This corresponds to the early social-smile milestone.
- E. 6 months — Incorrect. Social smiling should be present much earlier.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Social smile: approximately 6–8 weeks / 2 months.
- Lack of social responsiveness or smiling by around 2 months warrants developmental assessment.
- Check vision, hearing, interaction, and general neurological status.

questions.stem: Which finding is expected around 2 months of age?

options.label: A
options.text: Begins to hold the head up when placed on the tummy

questions.correctAnswerText: Begins to hold the head up when placed on the tummy
questions.initialExplanation: Early head lifting in the prone position emerges in the first months; steady head control is expected later, around 4 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Head lifting in prone — Correct. This is an early gross motor skill described.
- B. Unsupported sitting — Incorrect. This is usually expected later in infancy.
- C. Running — Incorrect. This is a toddler skill.
- D. Hopping — Incorrect. This is a preschool gross motor skill.

- E. Independent walking — Incorrect. This is usually acquired much later, during the second year.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early head lifting precedes stable head control.
- Do not confuse early prone head lifting with complete head control.
- Assess tone and symmetry if head control is persistently poor.

questions.stem: By approximately what age should an infant demonstrate visual fixation and following sufficiently well that persistent absence is a red flag?
questions.correctAnswerText: 3 months
questions.initialExplanation: The red-flag clinical guidance identifies failure to fix and follow by about 3 months as a reason for assessment of vision and development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 3 months — Correct. Persistent absence of visual fixation and tracking by this age warrants evaluation.
- B. 12 months — Incorrect. Visual fixation and following should be established well before this.
- C. 3 years — Incorrect. Assessment should occur much earlier.

- D. 18 months — Incorrect. This would represent a major delay in recognizing a visual problem.
- E. 9 months — Incorrect. This is too late to wait before investigating absent visual tracking.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fixing and following: an early visual milestone.
- Persistent absence by about 3 months is a red flag.
- Consider ocular, visual pathway, neurological, and developmental causes.

questions.stem: Which response is expected in early infancy?

options.label: E
options.text: Startling or reacting to a loud sound

questions.correctAnswerText: Startling or reacting to a loud sound
questions.initialExplanation: A young infant should respond to loud sounds, and later begins turning toward a sound or familiar voice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Short story — Incorrect. This is a preschool expressive-language skill.
- B. Two-step command — Incorrect. This requires later receptive language.
- C. Book questions — Incorrect. This is a later language/cognitive skill.

- D. Naming body parts — Incorrect. This is a toddler language milestone.
- E. Response to loud sound — Correct. This is an early hearing-related response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early infancy: startle or react to loud noise.
- Later: turn toward a sound and respond to voice.
- Absent response to sound requires hearing assessment; do not assume it is simply a language delay.

questions.stem: Which vocal behavior is typical during early infancy around 2 months?

options.label: B
options.text: Cooing and making sounds other than crying

questions.correctAnswerText: Cooing and making sounds other than crying
questions.initialExplanation: Early vocal development includes cooing and spontaneous vocalizations before canonical babbling and meaningful words.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Naming colors — Incorrect. This is a later cognitive-language milestone.

- B. Cooing — Correct. This is typical early expressive communication.
- C. “Why” questions — Incorrect. This is a later language milestone.
- D. Three-word sentences — Incorrect. These appear much later, around the preschool/toddler transition.
- E. Storytelling — Incorrect. This is a preschool skill.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early vocalization: cooing.
- Babbling develops later, with consonant-vowel combinations during infancy.
- Language milestones should be interpreted together with hearing and social communication.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant still has marked head lag and cannot maintain head control. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: It can be ignored until school age

options.label: B
options.text: This is a gross motor red flag requiring assessment

options.label: D
options.text: It is diagnostic of cerebral palsy by itself

options.label: E
options.text: This is expected in each healthy 4-month-old

questions.correctAnswerText: This is a gross motor red flag requiring assessment
questions.initialExplanation: The red-flag clinical guidance lists head control by 4 months; persistent marked head lag or poor head control warrants neurological and developmental assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ignore until school — Incorrect. Early assessment and intervention are important.

- B. Gross motor red flag — Correct. This finding needs evaluation of tone, strength, neurological status, and overall development.
- C. Advanced development — Incorrect. Persistent head lag is delayed, not advanced.
- D. Diagnostic of cerebral palsy alone — Incorrect. It is a concerning sign but has multiple possible causes and is not diagnostic alone.
- E. Expected in every infant — Incorrect. Head control should be substantially improving by this age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Head control is expected by around 4 months.
- Assess tone, symmetry, posture, and other developmental domains.
- One abnormal sign triggers assessment; it does not establish a single diagnosis.

questions.stem: During a developmental examination, which change is expected as head control matures toward 4 months?

options.label: B
options.text: The infant develops a mature pencil grip

options.label: D
options.text: The infant holds the head more steadily in supported sitting and shows much less head lag on pull-to-sit

options.label: E
options.text: The infant loses the ability to lift the head in prone

questions.correctAnswerText: The infant holds the head more steadily in supported sitting and shows much less head lag on pull-to-sit
questions.initialExplanation: Head control progresses during early infancy; by around 4 months, the head should be much steadier during handling and pull-to-sit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sentences — Incorrect. This is a later language skill.

- B. Pencil grip — Incorrect. This is a later fine motor skill.
- C. Running — Incorrect. This is a later gross motor milestone.
- D. Improved head control — Correct. This reflects maturation of neck and trunk control.
- E. Loss of prone head lifting — Incorrect. This would represent regression or weakness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Head control is an early gross motor milestone.
- Look for persistent head lag, hypotonia, asymmetry, or loss of previously acquired control.
- Corrected age may be relevant in premature infants.

questions.stem: Which fine motor/visual behavior emerges during the early months?

options.label: D
options.text: Looking at the hands and beginning to reach toward objects

questions.correctAnswerText: Looking at the hands and beginning to reach toward objects
questions.initialExplanation: Visual attention to the hands and reaching for nearby objects are early components of visuomotor development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Using a knife — Incorrect. This is a later self-care skill and requires mature coordination and safety awareness.

- B. Drawing a square — Incorrect. This is a later preschool fine motor skill.
- C. Tying shoelaces — Incorrect. This is a much later self-care skill.
- D. Hand regard and reaching — Correct. These are early skills linking visual attention with arm movement.
- E. Writing full name — Incorrect. This is a school-readiness skill.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early visual-motor development includes fixation, tracking, hand regard, and reaching.
- Reaching should become increasingly purposeful over the first 6 months.
- Assess whether both hands are used symmetrically.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the progression of motor skills during the first 6 months?

options.label: D
options.text: Stair climbing is a neonatal milestone

options.label: E
options.text: Head control and rolling emerge before independent walking

questions.correctAnswerText: Head control and rolling emerge before independent walking
questions.initialExplanation: Gross motor development follows a sequence from head control and rolling to sitting, standing, and walking.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Walking before head control — Incorrect. This reverses the normal developmental sequence.
- B. Hopping before sitting — Incorrect. Hopping is a much later gross motor skill.
- C. Tricycle before rolling — Incorrect. Tricycle riding is a later preschool skill.

- D. Stair climbing as a neonatal skill — Incorrect. Stair climbing is acquired in toddlerhood.
- E. Developmental sequence — Correct. Early postural control and rolling precede later mobility milestones.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Milestones develop in a broadly predictable sequence, although exact timing varies.
- Evaluate the quality and progression of skills, not only the final achievement.
- Loss of an established skill is a red flag at any age.

## Later Infancy: 8 to 12 Months

questions.stem: Which gross motor skill is commonly present by around 6 months?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rolling from tummy to back
questions.initialExplanation: Rolling from tummy to back is a common gross motor milestone around 6 months; rolling in both directions develops during later infancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hopping — Incorrect. This is a preschool milestone.
- B. Rolling tummy to back — Correct. This is listed summary around 6 months.
- C. Tricycle — Incorrect. This is a later preschool gross motor skill.

- D. Independent stair climbing — Incorrect. This occurs much later and initially with support.
- E. Running smoothly — Incorrect. Running is a later toddler skill.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rolling is an early mobility milestone.
- The source places rolling in the 6–8 month period.
- Assess symmetry and limb use while observing rolling.

questions.stem: Which behavior is expected as an infant's purposeful hand use develops around 6 months?

options.label: A
options.text: Reaching for an object and bringing it to the mouth

questions.correctAnswerText: Reaching for an object and bringing it to the mouth
questions.initialExplanation: Reaching, grasping, and mouthing objects are common exploratory and fine motor behaviors in later early infancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Reaching and mouthing — Correct. These behaviors demonstrate increasing hand control and exploration.
- B. Copying a square — Incorrect. This is a preschool/early school-age visual-motor skill.

- C. Shoelaces — Incorrect. This is a later self-care skill.
- D. Writing letters — Incorrect. This is a much later fine motor skill.
- E. Scissors — Incorrect. This requires more mature hand coordination.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Around 6 months, infants reach for wanted objects and explore them orally.
- Mouthing is common but requires choking-hazard precautions.
- Assess reaching with both hands.

questions.stem: Transferring an object from one hand to the other is an important milestone in which developmental domain?
questions.correctAnswerText: Fine motor development
questions.initialExplanation: Hand-to-hand transfer demonstrates improving voluntary grasp, coordination, and bilateral hand use.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fine motor — Correct. Object manipulation and transfer are hand-skill milestones.
- B. Social-emotional only — Incorrect. Social interaction may occur during play, but the motor skill itself is fine motor.
- C. Adaptive hearing — Incorrect. Hearing does not describe hand transfer.

- D. Gross motor — Incorrect. Gross motor skills concern posture and large movements.
- E. Expressive language — Incorrect. This involves spoken or signed communication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transfer emerges during later infancy, commonly around 6–9 months.
- standard guidance's red-flag table expects transfer by around 9 months.
- Persistent failure or marked asymmetry warrants assessment.

questions.stem: By approximately what age should an infant be able to sit unsupported?
questions.correctAnswerText: 9 months
questions.initialExplanation: The red-flag clinical guidance identifies unsupported sitting by about 9 months; persistent inability at this age warrants assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 9 months — Correct. Unsupported sitting is the milestone/threshold identified.
- B. 6 months — Incorrect. Many infants sit with support or tripod posture; stable independent sitting is later.
- C. 2 years — Incorrect. This is far beyond the expected age.

- D. 15 months — Incorrect. Waiting until this age would delay assessment.
- E. 3 months — Incorrect. Head control is developing at this age, but unsupported sitting is not expected.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sitting with support precedes independent sitting.
- Independent sitting is expected by around 9 months.
- Assess trunk control, tone, symmetry, and other developmental domains.

- B. Storytelling — Incorrect. This is a later language skill.

questions.stem: Stranger anxiety commonly becomes evident during which period?

options.label: D
options.text: It is not usually a normal developmental behavior

questions.correctAnswerText: Later infancy, often around 6–9 months
questions.initialExplanation: Stranger anxiety is a common social-emotional response during later infancy as infants increasingly distinguish familiar caregivers from unfamiliar people.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. At birth — Incorrect. Newborns do not show the typical later-infant stranger anxiety pattern.
- B. After 5 years — Incorrect. It commonly appears much earlier.
- C. Later infancy — Correct. Stranger anxiety often appears in the second half of the first year, with wide individual variation.
- D. Never normal — Incorrect. Stranger anxiety can be a normal developmental behavior.

- E. Adolescence — Incorrect. This is not the usual developmental period.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stranger anxiety and separation anxiety can occur in later infancy.
- Do not use absence of stranger anxiety alone as a developmental red flag.
- Assess reciprocal interaction, attachment behavior, and communication.

questions.stem: At approximately what age should a mature pincer grasp be developing?
questions.correctAnswerText: 12 months
questions.initialExplanation: The pincer grasp develops toward the end of the first year; the red-flag clinical guidance lists pincer grip by around 12 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 12 months — Correct. Pincer grasp is expected around the end of the first year.
- B. 3 years — Incorrect. Waiting until this age would miss an important fine motor red flag.

- C. 6 months — Incorrect. Palmar grasp and reaching are more typical at this age.
- D. 4 months — Incorrect. Infants are beginning to reach and grasp, not use a mature pincer grip.
- E. 2 months — Incorrect. Voluntary fine motor control is still immature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palmar grasp precedes pincer grasp.
- Pincer grip uses thumb and index finger.
- Lack of pincer grasp by around 12–15 months warrants assessment.

questions.stem: Which skill commonly emerges around 12 months and supports early communication?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pointing with the index finger
questions.initialExplanation: Pointing is an important gesture used to request, share interest, and direct another person's attention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Triangle — Incorrect. This is a much later drawing skill.
- B. Writing a name — Incorrect. This is a school-readiness skill.
- C. Index-finger pointing — Correct. This is a communication and fine motor milestone around the end of the first year.
- D. Scissors — Incorrect. This requires more mature fine motor control.
- E. Shoelaces — Incorrect. This is a later self-care skill.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pointing has communicative significance, not just motor significance.
- Assess both pointing to request and pointing to share interest.
- Absence of gestures/pointing by 12–18 months is concerning, especially with poor joint attention.

options.label: D
options.text: Pulling to stand and moving along furniture while holding on

options.label: E

questions.initialExplanation: Around 12 months, many infants pull to stand and cruise along furniture; independent walking may emerge later and varies between children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Tricycle — Incorrect. This is a preschool milestone.
- B. Running — Incorrect. This develops during toddlerhood.
- C. Hopping — Incorrect. This is a later preschool skill.
- D. Pulling to stand/cruising — Correct. This is a typical late-infant gross motor pattern.

## Toddler Milestones: 15 to 18 Months

questions.stem: Which description best fits the early walking pattern around 15 months?

options.label: A
options.text: Walks independently, often with a broad-based or initially unsteady gait

options.label: D
options.text: Walks downstairs with alternating feet independently

questions.correctAnswerText: Walks independently, often with a broad-based or initially unsteady gait
questions.initialExplanation: Early independent walking often appears around 12–15 months and may initially be broad-based and unsteady.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Early independent gait — Correct. This matches standard guidance description of early walking.
- B. Hops — Incorrect. Hopping is usually a preschool milestone.
- C. Runs and skips — Incorrect. These are more advanced skills.
- D. Alternating stair descent — Incorrect. This requires more mature balance and coordination.
- E. Tricycle — Incorrect. This is a later preschool skill.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early gait may be broad-based with arms held out for balance.
- Gait becomes more stable with practice.
- Failure to walk independently by 18 months is a developmental red flag.

questions.stem: A child aged 18 months is not yet walking independently. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: No assessment is needed if the child has a good appetite

options.label: C
options.text: This is typically normal until 3 years

options.label: D
options.text: It confirms a specific neuromuscular diagnosis

options.label: E
options.text: This is a gross motor red flag and should prompt developmental assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: This is a gross motor red flag and should prompt developmental assessment
questions.initialExplanation: The red-flag clinical guidance identifies independent walking by around 18 months; failure to achieve it requires assessment of motor development and possible underlying causes.

- A. Appetite excludes delay — Incorrect. Appetite does not rule out motor or neurological disorders.

- B. Language only — Incorrect. Walking is a gross motor milestone.
- C. Normal until 3 years — Incorrect. Waiting this long would delay evaluation.
- D. Confirms a specific diagnosis — Incorrect. It is a warning sign, not a diagnosis.
- E. Red flag — Correct. Assess tone, strength, joint range, symmetry, history, and other developmental domains.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Independent walking by 18 months is an important red-flag threshold.
- Assess for hypotonia, weakness, asymmetry, and regression.
- Early referral and intervention should not wait for a final etiological diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has persistent marked head lag and cannot maintain head control. Which developmental domain is primarily affected?

- D. Toileting — Incorrect. Toileting is a later adaptive skill.

- E. Social play — Incorrect. Social development involves interaction and reciprocal play.
questions.highYieldPoints:

- Persistent head lag, poor tone, or asymmetry should prompt assessment.
- This sign is not diagnostic of a specific disease by itself.
